newsitem.title: USA: Key items expected in Clinton FY98 budget proposal.
newsitem.headline: Key items expected in Clinton FY98 budget proposal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget proposal, to be made public on Feb. 6, was expected to take the following broad lines, according to administration officials who asked not to be identified.

TAXES: Clinton was expected to propose about $100 billion in tax cuts over five years. This would be partly offset by roughly $80 billion in revenue-raising measures, including restoring an expired airport excise tax and closing a variety of corporate tax loopholes.
On the tax cuts, officials said Clinton would hew closely to his fiscal 1997 proposals, adding to them tax initiatives unveiled in the 1996 presidential election campaign.

These included offering a $1,500 tax credit for college tuition and raising the capital gains tax exclusion on home sales to $250,000 per person, or $500,000 per couple, for all Americans. At present, there is a $125,000 capital gains tax exclusion only for taxpayers over 55.

They also included giving companies that hire someone who has been on welfare for at least 18 months a tax credit worth up to $5,000, or 50 percent of the first $10,000 in wages, health care or training provided to the employee.
MEDICARE: Clinton has said he will propose $100 billion worth of savings over five years from Medicare, which funds health care for the elderly, or $138 billion over six years.
Clinton, who unveiled the offer on Jan. 21, described it as meeting the Republicans halfway on the contentious matter, which was a major issue in the 1996 election campaign.

Officials said the figure compared to the $116 billion in cuts over six years that Clinton had proposed last year, as calculated by the Congressional Budget Office, and the $158 billion in cuts that the Republicans had put forward.

The savings would chiefly come from health care providers like hospitals, who would lose some $45 billion in payments over the six-year period, as well as managed health care plans, which would lose about $46 billion.

Medicare is a politically charged subject because of the president's success during the election campaign of painting Republicans as advocating severe cuts in the popular programme, which funds health care for 38 milliion people.

WELFARE: The administration plans to seek to restore more than $16 billion in spending cut by the welfare reform bill that Clinton signed into law last August. Much of this would be spent to restore foodstamp and other benefits to legal immigrants who were targeted in the law.
MEDICAID: The budget proposal seeks $20 billion in savings over five years, achieving these in part by imposing a cap on spending per recipient of the programme, which funds health care for the poor.
